content: Programs should be systematically monitored to ensure their effectiveness and safety. The impact of intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) can be assessed using routine data from hospital deliveries, clinics, and community health workers. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends using the Chemoprevention Efficacy Study (CPES) protocol to evaluate the efficacy of medicines used for chemoprevention. While molecular markers associated with treatment outcomes can be analyzed to monitor the potential impact of chemoprevention on drug resistance, the relationship between these markers and the efficacy of antimalarials for chemoprevention remains unclear, necessitating cautious interpretation of results. Despite high levels of resistance to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) in some areas, SP continues to yield positive outcomes for maternal and fetal health. National malaria programs may consider continuing IPTp-SP programs even in the face of declining efficacy for malaria-specific outcomes. Research gaps exist regarding IPTp, but these should not hinder the adoption and implementation of community-based approaches to improve uptake and address inequities in coverage. WHO will review data on the safety and effectiveness of alternatives to SP for IPTp when relevant meta-analyses become available. Even in regions with significant SP resistance, SP has shown benefits in improving fetal growth and reducing maternal anemia, potentially through non-malarial pathways. This aligns with findings from a meta-analysis of individual patient data from six trials comparing IPTp with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHP) versus IPTp with SP. While DHP was more effective in reducing malaria in areas of high SP resistance, it did not lead to better pregnancy outcomes, as SP was associated with improved fetal growth and higher mean birth weights. This may be due to the broad-spectrum antimicrobial properties of sulfadoxine, its impact on the maternal gut microbiome, or its ability to reduce inflammation. Perennial malaria chemoprevention (PMC), previously known as intermittent preventive treatment in infants (IPTi), involves administering a full course of antimalarial medication at predefined intervals, regardless of infection status, to prevent illness in settings with moderate to high perennial malaria transmission. The goal of PMC is to protect young children by maintaining preventive antimalarial drug concentrations in the blood, clearing existing infections, and preventing new ones during the period of highest risk for severe malaria. The updated recommendation expands PMC beyond infants to include children aged 12 to 24 months, reflecting the broader applicability of the intervention. WHO recommends that medicines used for PMC differ from those used as first-line malaria treatments. SP has been widely used for chemoprevention in Africa and has demonstrated efficacy, safety, tolerability, availability, and affordability. However, while artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) have been effective for PMC, evidence on their safety, efficacy, adherence to multi-day regimens, and cost-effectiveness in young children is limited. A single-dose regimen, such as SP, is preferable to multi-day regimens. The target age group for PMC should be determined using local data on the age distribution of malaria admissions and severe disease. While PMC was initially recommended for infants under 12 months, additional data have shown its value in children aged 12 to 24 months. Evidence from seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) programs suggests that the impact of chemoprevention on disease burden can be sustained beyond infancy with additional doses. However, there is limited information on the safety and efficacy of PMC in children older than 15 months in perennial transmission settings. Children at increased risk of severe disease should receive a complete course of antimalarials at the recommended treatment dose as part of PMC. Dosage should ideally be determined by the child’s weight, with age-based dosing used only when weight is unknown. The PMC schedule should be informed by the duration of protective efficacy of the selected drug and the feasibility of delivering additional courses. SP doses should be administered at least one month apart. Trials have evaluated various dosing regimens for SP in the first and second years of life, demonstrating its safety and impact. PMC programs should be routinely monitored for safety and effectiveness. In areas of moderate to high perennial malaria transmission, children at high risk of severe malaria can be given antimalarial medicines at predefined intervals to reduce disease burden. PMC schedules should consider the age pattern of severe malaria admissions, the duration of drug protection, and the feasibility and affordability of delivering additional courses. SP has been widely used for chemoprevention in Africa, including for PMC. While ACTs have been effective for PMC, evidence on their safety, efficacy, adherence, and cost-effectiveness is limited. The Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) platform remains important for delivering PMC, especially in the first year of life. Alternative delivery methods may be explored to optimize access to PMC and integrate it with other health interventions. The impact of drug resistance on the protection provided by PMC with SP is unclear. The duration of SP protection is reduced in settings with high parasite resistance mutations. While SP has shown efficacy in reducing clinical malaria in some settings, its overall protective effect diminishes in areas with high resistance. There is limited evidence that molecular markers predict the efficacy of PMC. PMC is not recommended for children with severe acute illness, those unable to take oral medication, those who recently received a dose of the drugs used for PMC, or those allergic to the drugs. PMC with SP should not be given to individuals receiving sulfa-based medications, such as co-trimoxazole. Information about PMC should be accessible to caregivers and stakeholders, and consent should be obtained from caregivers before administration. PMC is generally considered cost-effective due to its use of the EPI platform to deliver the inexpensive drug SP. However, it becomes less cost-effective in settings with lower malaria burden or with the use of more expensive medicines. The overall costs of implementing PMC with SP in children are moderate, and it is likely cost-effective compared to no intervention. The WHO recommendation for PMC was developed using the GRADE framework and informed by systematic reviews, contextual factors, and input from national malaria program representatives. The main outcomes of interest were the impact of PMC on confirmed clinical malaria and anemia. While the certainty of evidence ranged from low to high, the priority outcomes were assessed as moderate-certainty evidence.
